title: The Figure in the Measured Room: Stuttgart, the Bauhaus Stage, and the Lacquer Ballet
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Marquetry Bench and the Master's Class

stops.name: Stuttgart, the birth in the Kingdom of Wuerttemberg
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Neue Deutsche Biographie gives 4 September 1888 and the full name Oskar Alfred Victor. No birth address is recorded in any source reached, so the pin marks the historic centre of Stuttgart and not a house.
stops.campa: A last child is born to Carl Leopold Schlemmer and Luise Wilhelmine Neuhaus in Stuttgart and registered as Oskar Alfred Victor. The catalogues will spell him Oscar as often as Oskar, and neither spelling will settle. His father keeps no studio and no fortune; the household is the modest commercial Wuerttemberg of shopkeepers and clerks, and it does not hold together long. Within eighteen years both parents are dead, and the boy has been passed between a married sister's house and a workshop bench.
suggested_refs: Karin von Maur's Neue Deutsche Biographie entry, the standard biographical armature for the whole life
sources: Karin von Maur, Neue Deutsche Biographie, deutsche-biographie.de/gnd118608088.html

stops.name: Goeppingen, the married sister's house
stops.date_confidence: contested. German Wikipedia dates the move to Goeppingen to 1899 and the departure for Stuttgart to 1903; the working dossier for this file instead framed the move as a consequence of the father's death in 1902. The two cannot both be right and neither was confirmed to a document this pass. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He is sent east along the Fils to Goeppingen, to the house of his married sister Wilhelmine, and put to the Realschule there. Whether he goes before his father's death or because of it is exactly what the sources disagree about. What is not in dispute is the shape of it: a boy in another family's rooms in a small industrial town, doing school work he abandons at fifteen. He leaves for Stuttgart in 1903. His mother dies three years after that, when he is already gone.
suggested_refs: The Goeppingen Realschule registers, unexamined this pass

stops.name: Stuttgart, the intarsia bench at Woelfel und Kiessling
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1903-1905 by German Wikipedia and the Bauhaus Kooperation biography; the workshop's street address is not locatable, so the pin marks central Stuttgart. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Back in Stuttgart he apprentices as an applied-art draughtsman in the marquetry workshop of Woelfel und Kiessling, cutting and fitting veneers into patterns that must lie perfectly flat. The first training of his hand is inlay and not painting: a figure held inside a plane, edge meeting edge, no modelling and no depth, the contour carrying all of it. He is fifteen when he starts and seventeen when he leaves the bench. Where in Stuttgart the workshop actually stood, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: Surviving Stuttgart intarsia work of the 1900s, as context for the flat contoured figure

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Royal Academy and the scholarship
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1906 by the NDB and Bauhaus Kooperation; the month is an ordering device. Pin inherited from the canonical Stuttgart Academy coordinate already used in the atlas for the Hoelzel masterclass. The academy stood on Urbanstrasse in these years.
stops.campa: One semester at the Kunstgewerbeschule wins him a scholarship into the Koenigliche Akademie der Bildenden Kuenste, where he draws under Christian Landenberger and Friedrich von Keller before reaching the studio of Adolf Hoelzel, a theorist of colour teaching abstraction inside a royal academy. Somewhere in these years he meets a fellow student named Otto Meyer, and the friendship begun over a shared easel will run by letter until Meyer's death in 1933. No source reached this pass fixes the month they met.
suggested_refs: Adolf Hoelzel's colour teaching at Stuttgart, the common root of the later Bauhaus colour doctrine
sources: Kunstmuseum Basel, 'Otto Meyer-Amden / Oskar Schlemmer' exhibition text

stops.name: Berlin, the rooms of Der Sturm
stops.date_confidence: contested: German Wikipedia dates the move 1910/1911, the NDB 1911/1912. Month and day defaulted to 01. Pin marks Der Sturm's known Potsdamer Strasse address, not a residence of Schlemmer's.
stops.campa: He goes north to Berlin and works as a freelance painter with no institution behind him, near enough to Herwarth Walden's gallery and journal Der Sturm to see what is arriving from Paris: Cubism, the broken plane, the figure taken apart and set down again as facets. Stuttgart had given him Hoelzel's colour theory. Berlin gives him the evidence that a human body can be dismantled on canvas and still be read as a body. He is twenty-three and paints without buyers.
suggested_refs: Herwarth Walden's journal Der Sturm, 1910-1912 issues

segments.name: Hoelzel's Master Pupil and the Dancers

stops.name: Stuttgart, master pupil to Adolf Hoelzel
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1913 by German Wikipedia; the NDB independently dates the master-student status to the end of 1913, when three of Hoelzel's pupils are selected for the Werkbund murals. The working dossier's 1912 is one year early. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He returns to Stuttgart and is named master pupil to Hoelzel. The class around the old man is a small, quarrelsome company: Willi Baumeister, Hermann Stenner, Ida Kerkovius, and from the autumn a Swiss schoolmaster turned painter, Johannes Itten, who will carry Hoelzel's colour doctrine into the Bauhaus preliminary course years before Schlemmer ever sees Weimar. Otto Meyer has gone to the Swiss mountain village of Amden. The letters between them run from 1912 until Meyer's death in 1933.
suggested_refs: The Schlemmer-Meyer-Amden correspondence, 1912-1933, published in the Hueneke edition
sources: itten.journey.json, stop 1913-10-01, Stuttgart, the Academy and the masterclass of Adolf Hoelzel

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Neuer Kunstsalon am Neckartor
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1913 by German Wikipedia, which gives a run of roughly fifteen months. The gallery's street address is not recorded, so the pin marks the Neckartor district.
stops.campa: With his brother he opens the Neuer Kunstsalon am Neckartor, a room for advanced painting in a city that has almost none. He is twenty-four and running a gallery, which puts him on the far side of the wall from the painters for about fifteen months, and then the salon closes. It shows in that time what Stuttgart will not otherwise see. German Wikipedia names the co-founding brother as Wilhelm; the dossier that fed this file named Carl, and nothing reached this pass settles which of them stood at the door.
suggested_refs: Stuttgart exhibition notices, 1913-1914, for the Neuer Kunstsalon programme

stops.name: Stuttgart, the dancers Burger and Hoetzel
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date: the meeting is placed c.1912-1913 and more probably 1913, since Schlemmer only returns from Berlin in 1913. The frequently repeated detail that Burger and Hoetzel came from Jaques-Dalcroze's institute at Hellerau appears in no source reached this pass and is treated here as unsourced colour. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Two dancers, Albert Burger and Elsa Hoetzel, come to him in Stuttgart, and the three begin a project that has no name yet. Schlemmer sketches costumes: a wire hoop, a padded cone, a spiral of gilded card, bodies turned into solids of revolution and set moving inside a fixed cube of stage. It is not choreography as Stuttgart understands the word, and it is not painting either. Nine years of war and interruption pass before any audience sees the finished thing. The drawings survive the whole gap.
suggested_refs: The surviving Triadic Ballet costume figurines and design sheets, Staatsgalerie Stuttgart

stops.name: Cologne, twelve murals in van de Velde's theatre
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1914 by German Wikipedia and the Bauhaus Kooperation biography; the month marks the opening of the Werkbund exhibition and is an ordering device. Pin approximates the Deutz exhibition grounds, since the building no longer exists.
stops.campa: Hoelzel is given the decoration of the main hall of Henry van de Velde's theatre at the Werkbund exhibition and hands it to three of his pupils: Schlemmer, Baumeister, Stenner. Twelve murals go up inside a building conceived as an argument for the marriage of art and manufacture. It is Schlemmer's first architectural commission and his first wall. The exhibition closes early when the war begins in August. In 1922 the building is demolished with all twelve paintings still on it.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the van de Velde Werkbund theatre, Cologne 1914, before the 1922 demolition

segments.name: The War and the Three Dances

stops.name: The Western Front, the volunteer
stops.date_confidence: attested that he volunteers in 1914 and is wounded; the coordinate is an explicit placeholder on the French front and marks no battle, because no source consulted names one. Month set to the outbreak.
stops.campa: He volunteers at the outbreak of war and goes to the Western Front, where he is wounded twice. What happens next is disputed in the record. One account transfers him to a military mapping unit at Colmar in Alsace, drawing terrain for the guns; German Wikipedia sends him east instead, to service in Russia, and mentions Colmar nowhere. Neither version was confirmable this pass and neither is quietly preferred here. Four years of his twenties go to the army, and the costume drawings stay in a drawer in Stuttgart.
suggested_refs: German military service records for Schlemmer, 1914-1918, unexamined this pass

stops.name: Stuttgart, three dances on a December leave
stops.date_confidence: the date 17 December 1916 comes through the NDB-derived chronology and is carried as a reconstruction: the venue within Stuttgart is named in no source reached. The 1916 breakthrough paintings are attested by the Bauhaus Kooperation biography without a month.
stops.campa: On leave in December he meets Burger and Hoetzel again, and the three put three of the dances in front of an audience, reportedly at a charity evening tied to his regiment, to music by Enrico Bossi. The same period of leave produces the pictures that break him out of Hoelzel entirely: Bild K, Komposition auf Rosa, Geteilte Figur, the body reduced to a division of the picture plane. Then he goes back to the army. Which hall in Stuttgart held that first showing is nowhere written down.
suggested_refs: Enrico Bossi's score, used for the earliest documented performance of the Triadic material

stops.name: Stuttgart, the students elect their representative
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1918 by the NDB and German Wikipedia. The founding of the Ueecht group, described in the same campa, is attested to 1919. Pin inherited from the canonical Stuttgart Academy coordinate.
stops.campa: The armistice comes in November and the academy's students elect Schlemmer their representative. He uses the position to demand a modern curriculum and tries to bring Paul Klee to Stuttgart as a teacher. The faculty refuses. Klee goes to Weimar instead, and Schlemmer will follow him there within three years. The next year he and Baumeister found the Ueecht group, tied to the Berlin Novembergruppe, arguing in print for the reform of art teaching. Neither campaign changes anything in Stuttgart.
suggested_refs: The Ueecht group's 1919 statements on art-education reform
sources: paul_klee.journey.json, stop 1921-01-10, Weimar, the Bauhaus appointment

stops.name: Berlin, Der Sturm and the built figures
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1920 by the NDB, which names the works shown. The Galerie Arnold reception mentioned in the campa is dated only loosely to c.1919-1920.
stops.campa: Walden gives him a show in January. On the walls are Plan mit Figuren and constructions that are neither painting nor sculpture: Relief JG, Bauplastik R, figures built out into the room in wood and plaster and wire. Berlin reads him as a Constructivist and prints him as one, and Galerie Arnold in Dresden takes notice on the same terms, though the Dresden date is loose. He is not quite that. The geometry is a container for a body and not a replacement for it.
suggested_refs: Relief JG and Bauplastik R, the 1919-1920 constructions

stops.name: Stuttgart, the marriage to Helena Tutein
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1920 by the NDB and English Wikipedia; German Wikipedia specifies October, which is used here. Gropius's call to the Bauhaus is dated 1920 by German Wikipedia, with active service beginning January 1921.
stops.campa: He marries Helena Tutein in Stuttgart, known to everyone as Tut, trained in economics, from a Mannheim family. She will keep the household through unemployment, farm work and factory work, outlive him by forty-four years, and edit the letters and diaries that are now the principal source for everything he thought. The call from Walter Gropius in Weimar reaches him the same year, so the marriage and the Bauhaus begin in the same autumn. Three children arrive within five years. He is thirty-two, and the Weimar post will be the first salary of his life.
suggested_refs: Tut Schlemmer's edition, Briefe und Tagebuecher (Hatje, Stuttgart, 1958 and 1977)

stops.name: Weimar, called to the Staatliches Bauhaus
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Bauhaus Kooperation chronology dates active service to January 1921, the NDB gives the remit as wall design and sculpture together. The common description of Schlemmer as one of the first masters is loose, since the founding masters were appointed in 1919. Pin inherited from the canonical Weimar Bauhaus coordinate.
stops.campa: Gropius calls him to the Staatliches Bauhaus, and in January he takes up active service as a form master, for wall design and for sculpture at once. Paul Klee is appointed on the tenth of the same month. Johannes Itten has been running the preliminary course since 1919 and holds the mural workshop, which Schlemmer first shares with him and then inherits. The school is two years old and already fighting about what it is. His daughter Karin is born in Weimar that year.
suggested_refs: Bauhaus personnel records for the January 1921 appointments
sources: paul_klee.journey.json, stop 1921-01-10, Weimar, the Bauhaus appointment

stops.name: Stuttgart, Hindemith's one-act operas
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1921 by German Wikipedia; the month is an ordering device for a summer-leave commission. Coordinate is the Staatstheater Stuttgart at Oberer Schlossgarten 6. The exact correspondence of the one-act titles was not confirmed this pass.
stops.campa: On summer leave from Weimar he designs sets and costumes for Paul Hindemith's one-act operas at the Wuerttembergisches Landestheater in Stuttgart, the house he grew up beside. It is his first substantial paid work in a real theatre and it teaches him what a stage actually costs: sightlines, quick changes, an entrance that has to be made in four seconds, a performer who has to breathe inside whatever he builds around her. German Wikipedia names Franz Blei and Oskar Kokoschka as the librettists.
suggested_refs: Wuerttembergisches Landestheater programmes, 1921 Hindemith one-acts

stops.name: Weimar, Kandinsky takes the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1922 for Kandinsky's appointment; the transfer of wall-painting responsibility is attested in the NDB and Bauhaus institutional chronology without a month. Pin inherited from the canonical Weimar coordinate used for Kandinsky's own faculty stop.
stops.campa: Wassily Kandinsky arrives from Moscow by way of Berlin and is taken onto the faculty, and the wall-painting workshop passes to him. Schlemmer is freed for sculpture, life drawing and the stage, which is the work he came for. Kandinsky, Klee and Schlemmer now carry much of the school's teaching between them, three men who agree on very little about what a school of art is for. The handover of the workshop is recorded in the sources without a month. His second daughter, Ute-Jaina, is born in Weimar the same year.
suggested_refs: Bauhaus workshop assignments, Weimar 1922
sources: wassily_kandinsky.journey.json, stop 1922-06-01, Weimar, taken onto the Bauhaus faculty

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Triadic Ballet at the Kleines Haus
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: German Wikipedia's article on the Triadisches Ballett gives 30 September 1922, Kleines Haus of the Wuerttembergisches Landestheater, danced by Burger, Hoetzel and Schlemmer under the pseudonym Walter Schoppe. Coordinate is the Staatstheater Stuttgart building.
stops.campa: The Triadisches Ballett is danced complete at last, in the Kleines Haus of the Wuerttembergisches Landestheater: twelve dances, three performers, eighteen costumes of padded cloth, wire, glass and metal, in three parts running yellow, then rose, then black. Burger and Hoetzel dance it, and so does Schlemmer, billed under the name Walter Schoppe. The printed programme credits the work jointly to all three of them. Half the house hoots and half of it stands.
suggested_refs: The 30 September 1922 programme of the Wuerttembergisches Landestheater, Kleines Haus

stops.name: Weimar, the stage workshop and the painted wall
stops.date_confidence: attested: Bauhaus Kooperation gives 1923-1929 as his tenure of the Buehnenwerkstatt, after Lothar Schreyer's departure; the workshop-building wall decoration is dated 1923 by German Wikipedia, and its overpainting on Wilhelm Frick's order to 1930. Month defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Lothar Schreyer leaves and Schlemmer takes the Bauhaus stage workshop, the first department that is entirely his, and he will hold it for six years and through one move to another city. The same year he paints the wall decoration of the Weimar workshop building, figures in flat colour and relief running the length of the stair hall. In 1930 a Thuringian minister named Wilhelm Frick orders it painted over, three years before the party that shares his politics reaches Berlin.
stops.quote: The history of the theater is the history of the transfiguration of the human form
stops.quote_source: Oskar Schlemmer, 'Man and Art Figure', in The Theater of the Bauhaus, ed. Walter Gropius, trans. Arthur S. Wensinger (Wesleyan University Press, 1961); wording verified by full-text search of the Wensinger edition, no page number confirmed
suggested_refs: The Weimar Bauhaus workshop-building stair hall, decorated 1923, painted over 1930

stops.name: Weimar, the Nationaltheater in Bauhaus Week
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 August 1923 by German Wikipedia's Triadisches Ballett article, which places the Bauhaus Week performance at the Deutsches Nationaltheater and not at the school. Coordinate is the Nationaltheater, not the Bauhaus building.
stops.campa: For the Bauhaus exhibition week the Triadic Ballet is carried from Stuttgart to Weimar and danced on the sixteenth of August at the Deutsches Nationaltheater, because the school itself has no house big enough to hold it. The costumes go on tour inside the Bauhaus's first full public account of what it is for. Gropius wants the week to prove that the school makes objects. What goes onto the Nationaltheater stage on the sixteenth is eighteen costumes and three dancers.
suggested_refs: The 1923 Bauhaus Week programme, Weimar

stops.name: Dessau, the school moved and the essay written
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Bauhaus relocates to Dessau in 1925 and that Mensch und Kunstfigur appears in the fourth Bauhaus book, 1925; the month is an ordering device. Pin inherited from the canonical Dessau Bauhaus coordinate. His son Tilman is born in 1925, but the Weimar birthplace given in the dossier is doubtful, since the school is moving that year.
stops.campa: A hostile state government drives the school out of Weimar and it is rebuilt at Dessau, where Gropius raises the glass and concrete building that becomes its portrait. Schlemmer runs the Buehnenwerkstatt there as a department of its own and publishes Mensch und Kunstfigur in the fourth Bauhaus book, the essay that sets the living body against abstract space and declines to resolve them. He paints Roemisches, five figures in a room, and Konzentrische Gruppe. His son Tilman is born the same year.
stops.quote: Ich will Menschen-Typen schaffen und keine Portraets, und ich will das Wesen des Raumes und keine Interieurs.
stops.quote_source: Quoted with full citation in Karin von Maur, Oskar Schlemmer: Perspektiven des Menschenbildes, exhibition catalogue, Staatsgalerie Stuttgart, 1977, p. 9
suggested_refs: Bauhausbuecher 4, Die Buehne im Bauhaus (1925), containing Mensch und Kunstfigur

stops.name: Dessau, the letter about Mondrian
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 January 1926: a letter to Otto Meyer-Amden, cited with full bibliographic reference on German Wikipedia to Andreas Hueneke's edition of the letters, diaries and writings. Pin inherited from the canonical Dessau Bauhaus coordinate.
stops.campa: He writes to Otto Meyer-Amden in Switzerland, as he has written for thirteen years, and sets down what he thinks the school is actually built on. The Dutchman Piet Mondrian has never taught at the Bauhaus and has never set foot in Dessau. His rectangles and his three primaries are nonetheless in the furniture, the typography, the wall colours and the lettering on the doors. Schlemmer, who paints bodies and not rectangles, records the fact without complaint and without claiming it for himself.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Otto Meyer-Amden, 3 January 1926, in Andreas Hueneke (ed.), Oskar Schlemmer: Idealist der Form. Briefe, Tagebuecher, Schriften 1912-1943 (Reclam, Leipzig, 1990)
suggested_refs: The Hueneke edition of the letters, diaries and writings, 1912-1943

stops.name: Essen, the fountain room at the Folkwang
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1928-1930 by the NDB and German Wikipedia, which dates the destruction of the cycle to 1934. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the Museum Folkwang at Museumsplatz, corrected from a dossier pin that sat in central Essen.
stops.campa: For the Museum Folkwang he paints a cycle of nine mural compositions for a fountain room, the largest architectural commission of his life, figures standing and striding in shallow niches of colour. Ernst Gosebruch, the museum's director, has engaged Kirchner for the festival hall and Schlemmer for this. The work runs two years. In 1934 the regime has the whole cycle destroyed, and what remains of nine paintings is a handful of studies and a room that is no longer there.
suggested_refs: Photographs and studies for the Folkwang fountain-room cycle, destroyed 1934

stops.name: Darmstadt, the gold medal on the Mathildenhoehe
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929 by the NDB, which records both the gold medal and an honour prize at Der schoene Mensch in der neuen Kunst. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the Mathildenhoehe, corrected from a dossier pin about a kilometre south in central Darmstadt.
stops.campa: At the exhibition Der schoene Mensch in der neuen Kunst he is given a gold medal and an honour prize, the only state decoration of his life. This is the height of his official standing in Germany: a decorated painter of the human figure, forty-one years old, about to take a professorship, his ballet danced in three cities and his theory printed in a book with the school's name on the spine. Eight years later five or six of these same figures will hang in Munich as evidence of national degeneracy.
suggested_refs: The 1929 Darmstadt exhibition Der schoene Mensch in der neuen Kunst, Mathildenhoehe

stops.name: Dessau, the eleventh of July
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Bauhaus Kooperation biography: 'Er verliess das Bauhaus am 11.7.1929'. Pin inherited from the canonical Dessau Bauhaus coordinate.
stops.campa: He leaves the Bauhaus on the eleventh of July, four years after the move to Dessau and eight and a half after Gropius first called him. Hannes Meyer now runs the school on a line with little use for a stage department, the money is short, and Breslau has offered him a chair. He takes it. Nine years of Bauhaus teaching end as a date in a personnel file. The stage workshop does not survive his going in any form he would recognise, and the costumes and wire figures stay behind in Dessau.
suggested_refs: Bauhaus Dessau personnel file, departure of 11 July 1929

stops.name: Breslau, the professorship
stops.date_confidence: contested in detail: the NDB says he accepted the chair in 1928, German Wikipedia dates the appointment to June 1929, and his teaching runs 1929-1932. The month here is an ordering device for the start of teaching. The director is Oskar Moll, not Otto Moll as the dossier had it. Pin approximates the historic academy site in present-day Wroclaw.
stops.campa: He goes to the Staatliche Akademie fuer Kunst und Kunstgewerbe at Breslau, where the director Oskar Moll has assembled about the most modern faculty in Germany. Schlemmer takes the stage-art class and teaches under the heading Mensch und Raum, man and space, his own subject at last with his own name on it. He chairs the Silesian artists' association in 1931 and 1932. The record disagrees with itself about when he accepted: 1928 by one account, June 1929 by another, and both may be true of different pieces of paper.
suggested_refs: The Breslau Academy under Oskar Moll, 1926-1932

stops.name: Breslau, the two Stravinsky operas
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia attests two short Stravinsky operas staged in Breslau with Schlemmer's designs; the December 1929 dating and the identification as Le Rossignol and Renard come through the Museo Thyssen and NDB chronologies and were not independently confirmed this pass.
stops.campa: For the Breslau opera he designs two short Stravinsky works, Le Rossignol and Renard, the nightingale and the fox. Igor Stravinsky's animals are precisely the problem Schlemmer has been setting himself since the wire costumes: a singer is a body, a fox is a mask, and the stage has to make the second out of the first without lying about either. It is his first theatre work since leaving Dessau. Which two operas they were reaches this file only through the Thyssen and NDB chronologies; German Wikipedia records the designs and does not name the pieces.
suggested_refs: Breslau opera programmes, 1929-1930 season

stops.name: Berlin, the Kroll Opera and Die glueckliche Hand
stops.date_confidence: attested: German Wikipedia's article on Die glueckliche Hand gives the German premiere as 7 June 1930 at the Krolloper, Klemperer conducting, sets by Schlemmer. German Wikipedia's Schlemmer article calls the Schoenberg production his last staged work and dates it 1932, which is impossible, since the Kroll gave its final performance on 3 July 1931.
stops.campa: At the Kroll Opera in Berlin, Otto Klemperer conducting, Arnold Schoenberg's Die glueckliche Hand has its German premiere with sets by Schlemmer: coloured light, a stage that rises and falls, a man and a chimera and no realism at any point. The Kroll is the most advanced opera house in Europe and has thirteen months of life left before the Prussian state shuts it. One standard account calls this Schlemmer's final staged work and dates it to 1932. By 1932 the house is closed.
suggested_refs: Krolloper production records for Die glueckliche Hand, 7 June 1930

stops.name: Paris, the Concours de Choregraphie
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 July 1932 at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees by German Wikipedia's Triadisches Ballett article, with Alois Pachernegg's suite Deutsches Barock. Coordinate is the theatre itself.
stops.campa: He brings a reworked Triadic Ballet to the Concours de Choregraphie at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees, danced to Alois Pachernegg's suite Deutsches Barock. Paris in 1932 is where a European choreographic reputation is made, and this entry makes none. The ballet finds no company, no season and no repertory anywhere, and will spend the next forty-five years as costumes in storage and a folder of photographs. He goes home to a Germany that is seven months from Hitler.
suggested_refs: Concours de Choregraphie, Theatre des Champs-Elysees, 4 July 1932

stops.name: Breslau, the Bauhaus stairway
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1932 by the NDB and German Wikipedia, painted at Breslau on news of the Dessau Bauhaus's political closure; the month is an ordering device. The quote carried here is presented as Schlemmer's on German Wikipedia but with no book, letter or page cited there, and is therefore weaker than the file's other quotations.
stops.campa: News reaches Breslau that the Dessau Bauhaus has been shut by political order, and Schlemmer paints Bauhaustreppe: students climbing Gropius's staircase inside the glass building, faceless, in step, moving up and out of the top of the frame. Nothing in the picture mourns. The bodies are the same measured solids he has been building for fifteen years, set now on a real stair in a real building that no longer holds a school. The Breslau academy has months of its own left.
stops.quote: Wir brauchen Zahl, Mass und Gesetz als Wappnung und Ruestzeug, um nicht vom Chaos verschlungen zu werden.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Schlemmer on de.wikipedia.org, 'Oskar Schlemmer', in the discussion of the post-1931 railing figures; no book, letter or page is cited there
suggested_refs: Bauhaustreppe, 1932, oil on canvas, Museum of Modern Art, New York, accession 597.1942

stops.name: Berlin-Charlottenburg, the perspective class
stops.date_confidence: attested to summer 1932 by the Bauhaus Kooperation biography and German Wikipedia, following emergency-austerity closure of the Breslau academy; the month is an ordering device. Coordinate approximates the Hardenbergstrasse site, today the Universitaet der Kuenste.
stops.campa: Emergency austerity closes the Breslau academy and he is transferred to the Vereinigte Staatsschulen fuer freie und angewandte Kunst in Berlin-Charlottenburg to teach perspective. He picks the subject deliberately. Perspective is geometry, geometry has no faction, and a man who teaches vanishing points cannot easily be accused of a tendency. The calculation holds for about eight months. The press has already begun setting the word Bauhaus beside the phrase cultural Bolshevism, and his name appears in the same sentences.
suggested_refs: Vereinigte Staatsschulen fuer freie und angewandte Kunst, Berlin, teaching records 1932-1933

stops.name: Stuttgart, the retrospective closed and the painting sold
stops.date_confidence: the closure of the Wuerttembergischer Kunstverein retrospective before opening is attested by German Wikipedia and dated March 1933. The Philip Johnson purchase in Stuttgart in the same month is reconstruction: MoMA's provenance page returned 403 on every attempt this pass and the Wikipedia stub on Bauhaus Stairway carries no provenance section.
stops.campa: His first large retrospective, hung at the Wuerttembergischer Kunstverein, is closed by the new authorities before the public is let in. In the same city and, by the usual account, the same month, the American Philip Johnson buys Bauhaustreppe directly from him. The painting leaves for New York and Schlemmer keeps the money in a country where he can no longer show anything. That sale is reported everywhere and confirmed nowhere reachable: the museum's own provenance page refused to open this pass.
suggested_refs: MoMA provenance record for Bauhaus Stairway, 597.1942, inaccessible this pass

stops.name: Berlin, dismissed without notice
stops.date_confidence: contested: the NDB dates the dismissal to May 1933, other accounts to March. Both are recorded; neither is preferred here. Otto Meyer-Amden's death on 15 January 1933 is attested by German Wikipedia.
stops.campa: He is dismissed from the Berlin school without notice. The Neue Deutsche Biographie dates it to May and other accounts say March, and nothing reached this pass adjudicates between them. Either way he is forty-four, has three children, and has just lost the only salary he has. What follows is not exile. He does not leave Germany, does not have the money to leave, and spends the next ten years inside a country that has declared his work a disease. Otto Meyer-Amden died in January, and the estate is on his hands the same season.
suggested_refs: The Otto Meyer-Amden estate, administered by Schlemmer from 1933

stops.name: Dettighofen-Eichberg, the rented farm
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1933/1934 through 1937 by the NDB and German Wikipedia; the month is an ordering device. Coordinate is the municipality of Dettighofen, corrected from a dossier pin about 2.6 km east. The exact farmhouse site at Eichberg is not identified in any source reached.
stops.campa: The family rents a farmhouse at Eichberg by Dettighofen, a few kilometres from the Swiss border, and tries to live off the land: sheep, a garden, the work of people who have never farmed. The border is close enough to walk to and he does not cross it. Eichberg is not even one of the commune's three villages. It is a scrap of Buehl's territory attached to the district in 1936, which is to say the address barely is one. He paints very little here and sells less.
suggested_refs: Dettighofen parish and commune records for the Eichberg farm tenancy, 1933-1937

stops.name: Munich, the Degenerate Art exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested to 19 July 1937. The count of his works is contested: German Wikipedia says five paintings, the NDB says six, and both are carried. Pin inherited from the canonical atlas coordinate for the 1937 Munich exhibition; note that the show itself was staged in the Archaeologisches Institut in the Hofgarten arcades, not in the Haus der Kunst opposite.
stops.campa: The exhibition opens on the nineteenth of July in the Archaeologisches Institut under the Hofgarten arcades, across the way from the Haus der Kunst where the approved German art is hung. Five of Schlemmer's paintings are on the walls by German Wikipedia's count, six by the Neue Deutsche Biographie's, among them Roemisches and Konzentrische Gruppe in the first room on the ground floor. Some fifty further works of his are pulled out of German public collections that year.
suggested_refs: The 1937 Entartete Kunst exhibition catalogue and installation photographs

stops.name: Sehringen, the wooden house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the NDB, which records the move on 30 September 1937 after an inheritance received by Tut Schlemmer. Coordinate approximates Sehringen, a village of the Badenweiler commune, corrected from a dossier pin some three kilometres too far east.
stops.campa: An inheritance comes to Tut and the family leaves the rented farm for a wooden house and studio at Sehringen, a village in the hills above Badenweiler. He is forty-nine, banned from exhibiting, stripped out of every German public collection that held him, and he builds a studio. What comes out of it over the next six years has almost no buyer and is made anyway. It is the first property the Schlemmers have owned. They move in on the thirtieth of September.
suggested_refs: The Schlemmer house and studio at Sehringen, Badenweiler, from 1937

stops.name: Stuttgart, the painting firm and the camouflage
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1938 for the Albrecht Kaemmerer employment (German Wikipedia) and to 1939/1940 for the barracks camouflage work (NDB). Month and day defaulted to 01; the firm's address is not confirmed, so the pin marks central Stuttgart.
stops.campa: He takes work with the Stuttgart painting contractor Albrecht Kaemmerer, decorating buildings for a wage. German Wikipedia dates that employment to 1938, the Neue Deutsche Biographie the barracks work to 1939 and 1940. The man who spent twenty years making the human figure legible in measured space is now paid by the hour to cover a surface. On the barracks he lays down disruptive pattern, broken colour running across roof and wall, so that a pilot passing over cannot read where the building stops.
suggested_refs: Albrecht Kaemmerer painting firm, Stuttgart, employment records 1938-1940

stops.name: Wuppertal, the Maltechnikum of Kurt Herberts
stops.date_confidence: attested to October/November 1940 by the NDB and German Wikipedia. Coordinate approximates Wuppertal-Barmen, where the Herberts works stood; the exact factory address was not pinned this pass.
stops.campa: Kurt Herberts, who owns a lacquer works at Wuppertal, takes a group of banned artists onto his payroll in an experimental Maltechnikum: Schlemmer, Willi Baumeister, Georg Muche, Gerhard Marcks, Carl Grossberg. The stated purpose is research into paint technique and historical surfaces. The working function is shelter, a wage and a laboratory for men who cannot exhibit. From November he is on the payroll of a paint chemist, working on lacquer, patina and the behaviour of pigment on metal.
suggested_refs: The Wuppertal Arbeitskreis around Kurt Herberts, 1940-1943

stops.name: Wuppertal, the lacquer round-dance at the Barmer Theater
stops.date_confidence: attested to 6 December 1941 by German Wikipedia for the Herberts company's seventy-fifth anniversary performance; Schlemmer's own letter of 9 December 1941 describes it. Coordinate is an approximate placeholder for the Barmer Theater.
stops.campa: For the firm's seventy-fifth anniversary he builds a Reigen in Lack, a lacquer round-dance: six women in costumes of glass beads, beer mats and lacquered cardboard, a little over three minutes to a Handel sarabande, danced at the Barmer Theater. It is the Triadic Ballet remade out of factory offcuts for a paint company's birthday, nineteen years after Stuttgart. Three days later he writes to Tut about how it went, and about what an ordinary man in the audience asked him afterwards.
stops.quote: Sechs Damen, jede ein anderes Kostuem aus Glaskugeln, Bierdeckeln, Pappformen, etc. Sie machten es recht und schlecht. Mehr waere gar nicht moeglich gewesen. ... Die Gebildeten waren sehr angetan, der einfache Mann fragt: 'Was soll das bedeuten?' Aber das ist das Schicksal der Dinge.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Tut Schlemmer, Wuppertal, 9 December 1941, in Oskar Schlemmer: Briefe und Tagebuecher, ed. Tut Schlemmer (Hatje, Stuttgart, 1977), pp. 176-177
suggested_refs: The Lackballett costumes of 1941, preserved at Herberts's request
sources: Briefe und Tagebuecher, ed. Tut Schlemmer (1977), pp. 176-177

stops.name: Wuppertal, the eighteen window pictures
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1942 by the NDB and German Wikipedia; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Wuppertal is blacked out, and he paints eighteen small pictures called Fensterbilder, window pictures, out of what can be seen of lit interiors in the houses opposite: a figure at a table, a lamp, a shape crossing a room. Twenty years earlier he had built the human figure as a solid of revolution inside a measured cube of stage. He is looking at it now through glass, at night, from the street, at the size of a postcard. There are eighteen of them and they are the smallest works of his life.
suggested_refs: The eighteen Fensterbilder of 1942

stops.name: Baden-Baden, the last hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the NDB: died 13 April 1943 at Baden-Baden, cause given as Herzlaehmung. Hospitalizations at Stuttgart and Freiburg through 1942-1943 are attested by German Wikipedia; the contributing malnutrition is a family account, not a clinical record.
stops.campa: Diabetes and jaundice have had him in and out of hospitals at Stuttgart and Freiburg through 1942. In April he is admitted at Baden-Baden and dies there on the thirteenth, fifty-four years old, two years short of the end of the war. The Neue Deutsche Biographie records cardiac failure, Herzlaehmung. The family add malnutrition and inadequate wartime care to the account, against the shorthand of a plain heart attack that gets printed. What the family say rests on no clinical record that anyone has produced.
suggested_refs: The Baden-Baden death record, 13 April 1943

segments.name: The Painting, the Grave, and the Costumes

stops.name: New York, Bauhaustreppe at the Museum of Modern Art
stops.date_confidence: the museum holding is attested: Bauhaus Stairway, 1932, MoMA, accession 597.1942, an accession number consistent with a 1942 gift from Philip Johnson. The 1933 purchase from Schlemmer in Stuttgart is reconstruction only, since MoMA's provenance page returned 403 this pass. The date precedes Schlemmer's death by a year; the stop sits here because the painting's life runs separately from his. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Bauhaustreppe hangs in New York. Philip Johnson, who bought it in Stuttgart in the month the Nazis closed the Stuttgart retrospective, has had it on extended loan to the Museum of Modern Art and gives it outright, accession number 597.1942. A picture of students climbing into a school that had just been shut becomes the most reproduced image of the Bauhaus anywhere, in a city Schlemmer never saw. He is alive when the gift is recorded, at work in Wuppertal. Whether anyone told him, the record does not say either way.
suggested_refs: Bauhaus Stairway, Museum of Modern Art, New York, 597.1942

stops.name: Stuttgart, section 14 f2 of the Waldfriedhof
stops.date_confidence: the burial at the Stuttgart Waldfriedhof is attested by the NDB; the grave is section 14 f2, with Tut Schlemmer (1890-1987) in the same plot, per German Wikipedia's article on the cemetery. The exact date of the burial is not given in any source reached, so month and day here are a placeholder that only orders the segment.
stops.campa: He is buried in the Waldfriedhof at Stuttgart-Degerloch, section 14 f2, in the city he was born in and left and came back to eight or nine times across fifty-four years. Tut lives until 1987, edits the letters and diaries into the volumes on which nearly everything written about him now rests, and is laid in the same grave. The stone carries two dates forty-four years apart. What day in that spring the first burial took place, no source consulted records.
suggested_refs: Waldfriedhof Stuttgart-Degerloch, grave 14 f2

stops.name: Berlin, the Triadic Ballet danced again
stops.date_confidence: the 1970 television version (Bavaria Atelier for Suedfunk Stuttgart, 29 minutes, directed by Helmut Amann, advised by Tut Schlemmer, Ludwig Grote and Xanti Schawinsky) is attested by the Whitney Museum's event page; German Wikipedia credits the 1970 reconstruction to Margarete Hasting, a contradiction left standing. Bohner's 1977 Akademie der Kuenste commission is attested by tanzfonds.de. Coordinate is the Akademie's Hanseatenweg building in what was then West Berlin; its Pariser Platz house did not exist until 2005. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: No film of Schlemmer's own Triadic Ballet exists, and no complete notation of it survives. What travels instead are reconstructions: a colour television version of 1970, made with Tut Schlemmer advising, and in 1977 Gerhard Bohner's staging for the Akademie der Kuenste in West Berlin to music by Hans-Joachim Hespos, danced afterwards in more than eighty guest performances abroad and revived in 2014 by two of Bohner's own dancers. Every one of them works from photographs, costumes and the surviving figurines.
suggested_refs: Tanzfonds Erbe documentation of the Bohner reconstruction and its 2014 revival, tanzfonds.de

stops.name: Stuttgart, the settlement of 17 December 2024
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Oberlandesgericht Stuttgart's own press release, case 19 U 61/23 on appeal from Landgericht Stuttgart 7 O 266/09. The catalogue-raisonne warning quoted in the campa was read directly on schlemmer.org this pass; a further dossier claim about forged stage designs is not on that page and is dropped.
stops.campa: Twenty-two years of litigation among Tut Schlemmer's descendants over some sixteen hundred works, first before the Landgericht and then the Oberlandesgericht Stuttgart, end in a settlement rather than a judgment: the contested pictures are divided between the parties, some going to museums, and the forced auction that would have broken the estate apart is avoided. The estate's own catalogue warns separately that entries in the 1952, 1965 and 1979 catalogues may be incorrect or false, and that lost works have resurfaced carrying falsified provenance.
suggested_refs: Oberlandesgericht Stuttgart press release, case 19 U 61/23, 17 December 2024
